newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Gazprom has harsh words for Turkmenistan.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Gazprom has harsh words for Turkmenistan.

text.p: The head of Russia's natural gas monopoly Gazprom said the company might break off commercial ties with Turkmenistan, Interfax news agency said on Friday.
"We are ready to give up on Turkmenistan altogether," Interfax quoted Gazprom President Rem Vyakhirev as saying.

He also said Gazprom was ready to stop transporting Turkmen gas to Ukraine, saying that Gazprom itself could supply the Ukraine's energy needs rather than transporting Turkmen gas along its pipelines.
Gazprom's press office in Moscow could not immediately confirm the statements.
Turkmenistan is heavily reliant on Gazprom, because the Russian giant owns the gas pipelines linking Turkmenistan to Ukraine and, more importantly, countries outside the former Soviet Union.
Vyakhirev said he was due to meet Turkmen president Saparmurat Niyazov on August 6, and it was unclear to what extent his remarks were sabre-rattling ahead of the talks.

Niyazov is also due to meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Moscow on September 7, and the issue of gas transportation was expected to be one of a number of energy issues the two leaders were to have discussed.

Turkmenistan, with huge natural gas reserves but few independent export routes, has seen output and exports of the key hard currency earner plunge this year after a deal with Gazprom to transport its gas fell through.

The two sides signed an agreement in 1996 in which Turkmenistan was allowed to export 20 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas to Europe annually and another 20 bcm to former Soviet republics, including Ukraine.

With domestic demand for gas limited, the breakdown of relations between Turkmenistan and Gazprom, and separately Turkmenistan and Ukraine, has hit production hard. Turkmenistan produced only 0.55 bcm in June from 2.69 bcm in March.
Ukraine is said to owe the cash-strapped Central Asian country around $1 billion in unpaid gas debts.

Turkmenistan wants to build new gas export routes to Asia via Afghanistan or to Europe via Iran, but both routes are plagued by geo-political factors and cost huge sums which the impoverished former Soviet republic cannot raise alone.
